slides.heading: Seven letters, one climb, and the tone that needs them
body: Seven consonants, and every one of their sounds is already yours.
A shape to learn and a district to put it in.
One new tone, and these seven are what spell it.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Both halves of the name, out loud.
Seven shapes in one sitting, so write each one while its name is in your ear.

slides.heading: The third district, and the first letters to live in it
body: Harbour, market, and the hill above both.
The temple is the **high class**.
Today it goes from empty to seven residents.

slides.heading: The map from lesson seven, and what it promised
body: Seven sounds, two letters each. The harbour column has been yours since lesson seven.
Today the temple column arrives whole.
Each letter costs a shape and a tone, and the sound comes free.

slides.heading: First, the two that carry the most text
body: The seven arrive heaviest first.
The first two turn up within a page of almost anything.
One writes the everyday s, and the other writes h.

slides.heading: The tiger behind the gate
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **tiger**.
The same s as the chain's letter at the harbour, moved to the temple.
The monkey's shape with **one line crossed through it**.

slides.heading: The tiger's letter
body: The monkey's arching tail, and one bar across it.
Head at the base, the same as the monkey's.

slides.heading: The chest against the wall
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **chest**.
The owl's h, and this is the half of that pair the language actually uses.
The soldier's letter with a **kink in the left stroke**.

slides.heading: The chest's letter
body: A kink where the soldier climbs straight.
Then a loop, and a tall wall up the right.

slides.heading: Write both of them
body: The tiger: **the monkey, then one line across it**.
The chest: head, a kinked stroke down, a loop, a tall wall.
Six or seven each, name out loud.

slides.heading: What happens on the hill path
body: The monk comes from the temple, so he is **high class**.
The path **dips, then climbs**, which is the shape of the tone.
The other two stay level in their field. The monk is the one who goes up.

slides.heading: What a rising tone actually does
body: The pitch **dips, then climbs**, and finishes high.
The shape your voice makes on the English word *really*.
Skipping the dip gives you a different tone.

slides.prompt: Tiger, the long oo in the cellar, the snake closing it. The syllable alive, temple letter. **Out loud, with the dip, before you turn it over.**

answers: Rising, from the temple letter and the ending that leaves it alive.

slides.heading: Next, the three breathing letters
body: Three stops, all of them breathed. Your palm finds them.
Their harbour cousins are the buffalo, the elephant and the soldier.
Three shapes, each a letter you own with one change.

slides.heading: The egg in the alms bowl
body: The word means an **egg**.
The buffalo's kh, written from the temple.
The elephant's letter with **the tail taken off**.

slides.heading: The bag brought to the steps
body: The word means a **bag**.
The soldier's th, written from the temple.
The chicken's frame with a **head coiled inside it**.

slides.heading: The bee in the lotus
body: The word means a **bee**.
The tray's ph, written from the temple.
The tray's outline with **the head turned inward**.

slides.heading: Write all three
body: The egg: **the elephant, minus the tail**.
The bag: **the chicken, with a head coiled inside**.
The bee: **the tray, with the head turned in**.
Each one beside the letter it came from.

slides.prompt: Mast, the egg's letter, the long post. **Watch the order.** The mast goes down first and is spoken second. Work the tone out before you say it.

answers: Rising: temple letter, the syllable alive.
The same sound from the harbour would come out flat.

slides.heading: And the last two, which are rarer
body: The two rarest of the seven.
One of them opens the word a woman uses for *I*.
A half-learned letter gets read straight past, and the word goes wrong.

slides.heading: The cymbals on the step
body: The word means **finger-cymbals**.
The elephant's ch, written from the temple.
The mouse's profile, shortened, with **a flicked tail above**.

slides.heading: The lid on the shelf
body: The word means a **lid**.
The tooth's f, written from the temple.
The tooth's letter with **the head brought inside the rim**.

slides.heading: Write them, and then look at the two head turns together
body: The cymbals: **the mouse, shortened, with a flicked tail above**.
The lid: **the tooth, with the head brought in**.
Write the tray, the bee, the tooth and the lid in a row.
In both rows the harbour head hangs outside, and the temple head tucks in.

slides.heading: เ-ีย, the lodger who takes three rooms
body: Three marks, three rooms, **one vowel**.
The mast on the front steps, a mark on the roof, the giant's letter behind.
An **ee sliding into yah**, held long, in a single beat.

slides.heading: Write it around a consonant
body: Mast, consonant, the mark above, then the giant's letter.
Draw it left to right, say it consonant first.
More is written ahead of the consonant here than behind it.

slides.heading: And the short one
body: **เ-ียะ** — the same three stations, with the two hooks behind.
No common word uses it. Recognise the spelling and move on.
The long one keeps **all three marks in place** before a final consonant.

slides.prompt: Mast, tiger, the roof mark, the giant's letter. The syllable alive, temple letter. **Tone first, then out loud.**

answers: **เสีย** — to lose, to waste, to break.
Rising: temple letter, the syllable alive.

slides.prompt: Mast, boat, roof mark, giant's letter, mouse closing it. The boat lives at the **harbour**, and the ending hums. Say the tone out loud before you turn it over.

answers: Flat: harbour letter, the syllable alive.
Same vowel as the last word, and a different tone, from the district alone.

slides.heading: One word for each of the seven
body: **ของ** — of, or a thing. The egg's letter opening it.
**ฉัน** — I, the word a woman uses for herself. The cymbals.
**ถาม** — to ask. The bag, the long post, and the horse humming it shut.
**ถึง** — to reach, or to arrive at. The bag again.
**ผม** — I, the word a man uses. The bee, and the horse closing it.
**ฝัน** — to dream. The lid, and the mouse closing it.
**หา** — to look for. The chest, and the long post from lesson one.
**สูง** — tall. The tiger, and the long oo down in the cellar.

slides.prompt: เขา is read with a rising tone. Respell it with the water buffalo's letter in place of the egg's and the climb disappears. Same sound out of your mouth, same vowel — so what is that one written change doing?

answers: The district changed, and the district decides the tone.
Temple letter, the syllable alive, rising.
Harbour letter, the syllable alive, flat.
Two letters for one sound is how the script spells a tone.

slides.prompt: You hear a word pronounced with a breathed t at the front, a long open vowel, and a hum closing it — and the whole thing rises. Two letters in Thai write that breathed t. Which one is on the page, and how do you know?

answers: The bag's letter — the temple one.
The hum makes it alive, and alive plus temple gives rising.
The harbour letter would hand you a flat tone instead.
Hearing the tone tells you the spelling, with the word unseen.

slides.heading: Twenty-eight letters, and the temple open
body: Seven temple letters: **ส** tiger, **ห** chest, **ข** egg, **ถ** bag, **ผ** bee, **ฉ** cymbals, **ฝ** lid.
One rule for all of them so far: temple plus alive gives **rising**.
Write the column, with each harbour cousin beside it.
Next: six more doubled sounds, two at the temple and four at the harbour.
